screens.title: Concurrency and Parallelism in Distributed Systems
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of concurrency and parallelism as they appear in distributed systems. You will learn the precise difference between handling many tasks at once by interleaving steps versus performing work truly simultaneously, and why both matter when services span multiple machines. We'll explore common hazards—race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks—by walking through short, concrete examples that show how shared state goes wrong. Then we'll move to synchronization strategies: how local locks, distributed locks, and higher-level models like eventual consistency and conflict-free replicated data types let systems stay available while avoiding incorrect results. Finally you'll see patterns engineers use in practice, such as the transactional outbox, and a checklist for spotting when shared mutable state should be redesigned or guarded. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to identify concurrency risks in a distributed design and propose appropriate synchronization or consistency techniques. Think of this chapter as a toolkit: definitions, examples, and proven patterns you can apply during design interviews and real system work.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Concurrency is interleaved progress; parallelism is truly simultaneous work. Distributed systems need explicit coordination and careful consistency models to avoid subtle failures.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Concurrency & Parallelism
Concurrency vs Parallelism
Distinguish interleaved execution from true simultaneous execution and learn why distributed systems need both

Concurrency gives the system the ability to manage many tasks, often by interleaving operations. Parallelism uses multiple processors or machines to execute tasks at the same time. In distributed systems we combine both: concurrency to scale request handling, and parallelism to process large workloads across nodes.

Analogy
Juggling many tasks is concurrency. Multiple jugglers sharing the load is parallelism.
Why it matters
Design choices affect availability, latency, and correctness when nodes fail or messages reorder.
Explore Key Topics
Race Conditions
How concurrent access to shared state causes lost updates.
Distributed Locks
Coordination across nodes using a lock service and fencing tokens.
Consistency Models
Eventual consistency and CRDTs as alternatives to strict locking.
Visual Concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Concurrency: many interleaved flows sharing resources
Parallelism: multiple processors or nodes doing work at the same instant
Quick Orientation
Throughout this chapter we'll alternate definitions, small code or pseudo-code examples, and design patterns you can apply in interviews and systems design. Expect conceptual checks: a race condition illustration, lock-based solutions, and higher-level alternatives like CRDTs and the transactional outbox.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide our practical work. First, you'll be able to differentiate concurrency and parallelism in a system design context: describe how interleaving differs from true simultaneous execution and why that distinction changes your coordination choices. Second, you'll identify common concurrency hazards—race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks—by recognizing their symptomatic patterns and the typical causes when shared mutable state exists across threads or nodes. Third, you'll explain synchronization mechanisms: when to use locks, semaphores, or atomic operations on a single machine, and when distributed lock services or consensus are required. Fourth, you'll describe how distributed systems manage concurrency through distributed locks, eventual consistency, and CRDTs, and choose between them depending on availability and correctness requirements. Each objective pairs a skill with a short scenario so you can practice applying the concept to design decisions. By the end, you will not only name these techniques but also weigh trade-offs and recommend concrete solutions for interview-style problems.

screens.title: How to use these skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives page focuses on practical application. You'll practice diagnosing interview-style scenarios: spotting shared mutable state, deciding whether a lock or a consistency model is needed, and proposing a safe, available approach. For example, given two services updating the same product stock, you should recognize a race condition risk and justify a distributed lock or a redesign to remove shared writes. You'll also practice trade-offs: when eventual consistency or CRDTs are acceptable, and when strong coherence is required, like in financial systems. Finally we'll train you to propose concrete engineering choices: a lock service with fencing tokens, or an outbox pattern for safe messaging. These skills let you present clear, defensible choices in an interview and avoid common mistakes in real systems. By the end you will be able to map a system requirement to a concurrency control plan that balances correctness and availability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › How to use these skills
From diagnosis to a design decision
Interview scenario practice
  • Spot shared mutable state such as a central counter or stock value. Ask: who writes, who reads, and how often?
  • Decide whether a distributed lock is suitable or if redesign to remove the shared write is better for scalability.
  • When availability is primary, consider eventual consistency or CRDTs; when correctness is primary, choose stronger coordination.
Mnemonic
D-A-R-T: Detect, Assess, Recommend, Test. Detect shared state. Assess trade-offs. Recommend lock or model. Test failure modes.

screens.title: Defining Concurrency and Parallelism
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the two terms with clear, practical definitions. Concurrency is the system's ability to manage multiple tasks such that progress appears to happen at the same time; this is often achieved by interleaving work on a single processor or coordinating many tasks so the system is responsive. Parallelism is the true simultaneous execution of tasks using multiple processing units or machines. In practice, a web service uses concurrency to handle many client requests at once by switching between request handlers, while a batch job uses parallelism to split a large dataset across nodes for simultaneous processing. This distinction affects correctness and coordination because concurrency introduces interleaving that creates ordering uncertainty, while parallelism adds capacity and true simultaneous mutation possibility across independent processors. A common misconception is to believe that adding more threads or nodes automatically eliminates race conditions; it doesn't. If multiple workers modify the same shared value, interleaving or simultaneous execution can both produce incorrect final state unless guarded. As a quick example, consider a counter service: concurrency lets many requests be handled quickly but requires synchronization to avoid lost increments; parallelism scales throughput but also multiplies the need for coordination. The takeaway is simple: name the mode your design needs, then pick the coordination model that provides the required correctness guarantees.

keyIdea.title: Definition takeaway
keyIdea.text: Concurrency is interleaving; parallelism is simultaneous execution. Both require coordination when shared state exists.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Defining Concurrency & Parallelism
Terms and formal claims
Precise meanings reduce mistaken design choices. Concurrency concerns scheduling and interleaving; parallelism concerns physical simultaneous execution.
Concrete example
A single-core server that runs many threads is concurrent: handlers switch rapidly. A cluster processing parts of a dataset in parallel demonstrates parallelism.
Common misconception
More threads or machines alone won't ensure correctness; coordination is still required when state is shared.
Key Takeaway

Label whether you need concurrency, parallelism, or both before selecting synchronization primitives or consistency models.

Visual comparison
Concurrency
  • Interleaved tasks
  • Single or many cores
  • Requires scheduling
Parallelism
  • Truly simultaneous execution
  • Multiple processors or nodes
  • Increases capacity
Why it matters
Decisions about locks, consistency, and architecture all depend on whether operations can overlap in time and whether they run on the same runtime or across nodes.

screens.title: Race Conditions Explained
screens.narratorSegment: A race condition happens when the final outcome depends on the unpredictable order or timing of operations by concurrent actors. The essential characteristic is that two or more actors read and write the same mutable state without proper coordination. A typical illustration: two nodes attempt to increment a shared counter. Both read the same initial value, each computes the updated value, and each writes back. If the writes are not serialized, one increment can overwrite the other, leaving the counter lower than expected. This is not a timing bug only; it is a correctness bug rooted in shared mutable state. Concrete example: imagine a database counter at value ten. Node A reads ten and computes eleven, then pauses. Node B also reads ten and computes eleven, then writes eleven. When A resumes it writes eleven too. The system ends up at eleven instead of twelve. Common misconceptions include assuming database writes are atomic across reads and writes or believing that network latency only causes performance issues rather than correctness ones. To prevent races in single-process programs we use locks, atomic operations, or transactions. In distributed systems, an additional layer is needed: distributed locks or models that avoid shared mutable writes entirely, such as CRDTs or designing operations to be idempotent. The key takeaway: locate shared mutable state and force a single authoritative update path or use a mergeable model to avoid lost updates.

keyIdea.title: Race condition core
keyIdea.text: When multiple actors operate on the same mutable state without coordination, final results depend on interleaving and can be incorrect.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Race Conditions
Step-by-step illustration
1. Two nodes read a shared value concurrently.
2. Each computes an update independently.
3. Writes occur without serialization, causing one update to overwrite another.
Concrete scenario
Counter at 10. Node A reads 10, computes 11, pauses. Node B reads 10, computes 11, writes 11. Node A writes 11. Final value 11 instead of 12.
Pro-tip
Ask who owns the write path. If ownership is singular you can avoid global locks by routing writes to the owner node.
Prevention approaches
Single-machine
Use mutexes, semaphores, or atomic operations to protect critical sections.
Distributed
Use distributed locks, strong consensus, or switch to mergeable data types like CRDTs when partition tolerance is required.
Key Takeaway
Locate shared mutable state. Either serialize access or design replica-merge semantics to avoid lost updates.

screens.title: Deadlocks and Livelocks
screens.narratorSegment: Two additional hazards often appear when multiple actors coordinate: deadlocks and livelocks. A deadlock occurs when two or more processes each hold resources the others need and wait indefinitely; no one can make progress. A classic two-resource deadlock: process one holds resource A and waits for B while process two holds B and waits for A. That cycle of waiting is the defining pattern. Livelock looks similar but is distinguished by continuous state changes that nevertheless yield no forward progress; processes keep reacting to each other without making the intended updates. An example is two networked services that repeatedly back off and retry in reaction to each other's retries, never completing the operation. To avoid deadlocks, focus on resource ordering: impose a global order for acquiring locks so cycles cannot form, or use try-lock with rollback and retry logic. To mitigate livelock, introduce randomized backoff or change retry strategies so actors do not tightly synchronize their retries. In distributed systems, partial failures and network delays can turn benign lock sequences into deadlocks if timeouts are neglected. A common misconception is treating timeouts as mere performance knobs; they are essential safety mechanisms. The core takeaway: reason about progress and ordering, and design global acquisition rules or timeout-based recovery to preserve forward progress.

keyIdea.title: Progress focus
keyIdea.text: Deadlock prevents progress by waiting cycles; livelock prevents progress by continuous reaction. Design ordering and backoff to restore progress.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Deadlocks & Livelocks
Deadlock
Cycle of waiting for resources held by others. No one can proceed.
Example
Process A locks resource 1 then waits for resource 2. Process B locks resource 2 then waits for resource 1. Both wait forever.
Prevention
Impose a global lock ordering, use try-lock plus rollback, and set timeouts to recover from unexpected waits.
Livelock
Processes keep changing state in response to each other but never make progress.
Example
Two services repeatedly back off and retry at the same time, continuously adjusting but not completing the operation.
Mitigation
Add randomized backoff, jitter, or change retry logic to break synchronous reaction patterns and allow eventual progress.

screens.title: Synchronization Primitives and Their Limits
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronization primitives are the building blocks that prevent concurrent hazards on a single machine. Mutual exclusion locks or mutexes let only one thread enter a critical section at a time. Semaphores generalize this by allowing a fixed number of concurrent holders. Atomic operations, such as compare-and-swap, give lock-free guarantees for certain updates. While these primitives solve many problems on one host, they do not automatically work across machines: memory is local, and network partitions, latency, and partial failures break assumptions. For distributed coordination you need a shared, reliable service or a consensus mechanism that provides a consistent view of lock ownership. Another important limitation is performance: fine-grained locking can hurt throughput and increase contention; coarse-grained locking simplifies correctness but reduces parallelism. Deadlocks and priority inversion remain concerns even with correct locking. A recommended pattern is to minimize shared mutable state: prefer immutable messages, owner-based routing of writes, or partitioning so locks are local to a shard. When distributed locking is unavoidable, design for failure: use timeouts, fencing tokens to prevent stale lock holders from acting, and ensure the lock service itself is highly available and consistent. This mindset helps you judge when to use primitives and when to adopt alternative models.

keyIdea.text: Local synchronization primitives are powerful locally but need careful translation to the distributed setting; minimize shared state when possible.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Synchronization Primitives
Primitives
Mutex: exclusive access to a critical section.
Semaphore: allows N concurrent holders.
Atomic ops: lock-free updates for specific patterns.
Design note
Prefer lock-free or owner-based designs when contention will be high. Use coarse locks only when correctness complexity outweighs lost concurrency.
Why in-memory locks fail across nodes
  • Memory is local: a mutex on node A cannot prevent a write from node B.
  • Network partitions and crashes can leave locks stale unless timeouts and fencing are used.
  • Distributed lock managers are a separate dependency and must be highly available.
Key Takeaway
Treat distributed coordination as a service: plan for failures, timeouts, and ownership validation rather than assuming local primitives are sufficient.

screens.title: Distributed Locks: Patterns and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed locks extend the mutual exclusion concept across machines by using a centralized or consensus-backed service to grant ownership. Typical implementations use ZooKeeper, etcd, or Redis with a carefully designed algorithm. The basic workflow: a client requests a lock from the lock service, which grants ownership if the lock is free. The client performs the critical update while holding the lock, then releases it. Several pitfalls must be considered. First, the lock service must itself be highly available; if it fails, the system may block. Second, network partitions and client crashes can leave stale locks. To mitigate stale-holders performing banned operations after a timeout, fencing tokens are used: when a client acquires the lock it receives a monotonically increasing token from the lock service and includes it with its write. Lock-aware resources reject writes that carry older tokens. A common mistake is naive lock release: clients should only release locks they own, and implementations must verify ownership before deleting lock keys. If you use Redis, patterns like SETNX with expirations are simple but require care: ensure clock skew and expiry races are handled, or prefer a consensus-backed store for strict correctness. The practical takeaway is to prefer distributed locks when you must serialize access across nodes, and to pair locks with timeouts, fencing, and ownership checks to remain robust in the face of failures.

keyIdea.title: Lock service takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use a reliable lock service with timeouts and fencing tokens; design for stale holders and ownership verification.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Distributed Locks
Typical flow
  1. Client requests lock from the lock manager.
  2. Lock manager grants ownership and issues token.
  3. Client uses token to perform protected updates.
  4. Client releases lock; manager grants next waiter.
Fencing tokens
A token prevents stale clients from making writes after losing a lease. Resources reject older tokens to avoid state corruption.
Common mistake
Relying solely on key expiry without fencing can allow expired clients to perform late writes, corrupting state.
Tooling notes
ZooKeeper / etcd
Consensus-backed services that provide stronger guarantees for lock ownership and ordering.
Redis (SETNX/Redlock)
Simpler and fast, but requires careful expiry, ownership checks, and understanding of edge cases.
Key Takeaway
If you must serialize across nodes, use a lock service and fencing tokens, and design for failures and ownership verification.

screens.title: Eventual Consistency vs Strong Consistency
screens.narratorSegment: Consistency models govern the guarantees a system provides about reads after writes. Strong consistency guarantees that once a write completes, all subsequent reads will see that write. Eventual consistency relaxes this by guaranteeing that if no new updates are made, replicas will converge to the same value eventually. The trade-off is the familiar CAP tension: prioritizing availability and partition tolerance often requires relaxing immediate consistency. Which model you choose depends on your application's correctness needs. For social features such as like counts or view counters, eventual consistency is acceptable because temporary divergence is harmless and availability is important. Conversely, financial account balances demand strong consistency because even a small window of divergence can lead to incorrect balances or double-spends. A misconception is to treat eventual consistency as sloppy design; it is instead a deliberate choice that trades immediate coherence for availability and performance, often combined with conflict-resolution strategies. When using eventual consistency, pair it with monitoring and clear user expectations: show eventual values in UIs or provide conflict resolution semantics. The takeaway: pick the weakest consistency that still meets correctness requirements to maximize availability and performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Eventual vs Strong Consistency
Strong consistency
After a successful write, all subsequent reads return that write. Use when correctness cannot be compromised.
Use case
Banking and inventory where immediate correctness is required.
Eventual consistency
Replicas converge over time if no new updates occur. Use when temporary divergence is acceptable for higher availability.
Use case
Social feeds and counters where immediate sync across replicas is not critical.
Design guidance
  • Choose strong consistency for operations that must be correct immediately.
  • Choose eventual consistency when availability under partition is prioritized and application semantics tolerate divergence.
  • Combine eventual models with merge strategies or CRDTs to automate conflict resolution where needed.

screens.title: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs)
screens.narratorSegment: CRDTs are specially designed data types that can be replicated across multiple nodes and concurrently updated while guaranteeing that replicas converge without coordination. The key idea is to design merge rules that are associative, commutative, and idempotent so that the order of operations doesn't matter for the final state. Examples include grow-only counters, last-writer-wins registers, and sets with well-defined merge behavior. In a collaborative editor, CRDTs allow multiple users to edit simultaneously and have edits merged automatically without a global lock. The major advantage of CRDTs is availability: nodes can accept writes locally even during partitions and later reconcile deterministically. The trade-offs are complexity and sometimes imprecise semantics—some CRDTs, like last-writer-wins, discard information based on timestamps, which may be undesirable for some domains. Another misconception is thinking CRDTs replace all coordination; they are ideal when merge semantics fit application correctness. When strict serializability is required, CRDTs are not a substitute. The practical rule: when you can express your update intent as a mergeable operation and can tolerate the CRDT's semantics, they greatly simplify distributed concurrency by removing the need for synchronous locks.

keyIdea.title: CRDT takeaway

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › CRDTs
How they work
Design operations so merging concurrent updates is deterministic regardless of order.
Example types
Grow-only counter, last-writer-wins register, and add/remove sets with tombstones or version vectors.
When to use
Use CRDTs when you need high availability and deterministic merges and your application semantics match available merge rules.
Limitations and misconceptions
  • Not a substitute for strong serializability when that is required.
  • Merge semantics can be lossy, so choose CRDT types that match domain needs.
  • CRDTs can increase storage or metadata overhead (version vectors, tombstones).
Key Takeaway
Prefer CRDTs when automatic, conflict-free merging fits the application and when availability under partitions is essential.

screens.title: Transactional Outbox Pattern (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: The transactional outbox pattern solves a common distributed problem: ensuring a state update and an external message publication occur atomically. In many services you must update local state and then publish an event to a message broker; doing those operations separately can lead to inconsistencies if one succeeds and the other fails. The outbox pattern records the outgoing message in a local outbox table inside the same database transaction as the state change. After the transaction commits, a separate reliable process reads pending outbox entries and publishes them to the message broker, deleting entries only after successful publication. This decouples the atomicity of the state change from the eventual act of publishing, while guaranteeing that messages are not lost or duplicated beyond what the publisher handles. Important operational notes: the outbox reader must handle retries and idempotency, and visibility to the message system must be monitored. A common misconception is that the outbox removes the need for idempotent consumers; it does not — consumers still need to tolerate duplicates if the publisher retries. The practical outcome is a simpler failure model: updates are durable and messages are eventually published, letting services coordinate without distributed transactions across services.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Transactional Outbox
Pattern summary
Record outgoing messages in an outbox table within the same local transaction as the state change. A separate process publishes them.
Operational notes
The outbox reader must handle retries and ensure idempotent publishes. Monitor the outbox table to detect stuck entries.
Key Takeaway
The outbox gives atomic intent: either the state change and message were recorded, or neither was, simplifying recovery.
Conceptual pseudo-code
# Transactional outbox (conceptual Python-like pseudocode)
# Begin DB transaction
# Update service state
db.update_order_status(order_id, 'paid')
# Insert outbox message in same transaction
db.insert_outbox({ 'topic': 'order-paid', 'payload': { 'order_id': order_id } })
# Commit transaction

# Separate publisher process:
# Read unprocessed outbox rows
messages = db.read_pending_outbox()
for msg in messages:
  try:
    message_broker.publish(msg.topic, msg.payload)
    db.delete_outbox_entry(msg.id)
  except Exception:
    # Retry later; ensure idempotent publish on broker or include dedupe key
    continue
Misconception check
The outbox reduces cross-service transaction needs but does not remove the need for idempotent consumers or delivery guarantees from the messaging layer.

screens.title: Analyzing Concurrency in a Design Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: When presented with a system design or interview scenario, follow a short checklist to identify concurrency concerns and choose an appropriate mitigation. First, detect shared mutable state: ask which data items have multiple writers and where single writers could be introduced. Second, assess correctness requirements: does the application tolerate eventual convergence or require immediate consistency? Third, consider scale and latency: will locking degrade throughput or produce hotspots? Fourth, evaluate failure modes: what happens if a lock holder crashes or a network partition occurs? Based on these answers, recommend either local synchronization (if the problem is single-node), a distributed lock with fencing (if serialization across nodes is essential), or a consistency-based redesign such as CRDTs, owner-based writes, or the transactional outbox. A concrete example: two microservices updating a product's stock concurrently. Detect that both write the same field. If immediate consistency is required, propose a distributed lock keyed by product id and explain fencing and timeout handling. If availability is prioritized and small discrepancies are acceptable, suggest an eventual model or partitioned ownership per product shard. Finally, verify your choice by outlining recovery steps for crashes and how to monitor integrity. The takeaway is to follow a repeatable checklist to produce a defensible recommendation.

  2. Assess correctness: is immediate consistency required?
  3. Estimate contention and scale: will locks become a bottleneck?
  4. Plan for failures: timeouts, fencing, and recovery steps.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Engineers often make a small set of recurring mistakes when reasoning about distributed concurrency. One is assuming networked operations are atomic; a write to a remote database may succeed on one replica and fail on another, producing partial effects. Another is neglecting partial failure: a client may acquire a lock then crash, leaving the resource held unless leases and timeouts are used. A third mistake is underestimating message ordering and latency—assuming a later update cannot overtake an earlier one across replicas. To avoid these, explicitly model failure modes in your design: what happens if a leader crashes, a lock service becomes unavailable, or messages reorder? Use timeouts and fencing for locks, ensure idempotent operations and at-least-once or exactly-once publishing where appropriate, and monitor for anomalies in replica divergence. Common quick checks in reviews include asking how ownership is transferred, how stale writers are protected against, and whether your design permits lost updates under high latency. A useful safety principle is to minimize shared mutable state or confine it to a single owner when possible. When unavoidable, build defensive patterns: timeouts, fencing tokens, transactional outbox, and observability to detect when models diverge. The core message: designing for failure is the point of distributed concurrency planning.

Frequent mistakes
  • Treating remote writes as atomic across replicas.
  • Not planning for stale lock holders or crashed clients.
  • Assuming message ordering across partitions is preserved.
Reviewer checklist

Defensive patterns
Fencing & timeouts
Prevent stale holders from making late writes and recover from crashed clients.
Idempotency
Make consumers tolerant of duplicate messages to simplify retry strategies.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Activity: Simulate a Race and Apply a Distributed Lock (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: This activity guides you through a conceptual simulation and a lock-based solution for a distributed counter. First, illustrate the race: two nodes read the same counter value, compute increments, and write without coordination, producing a lost update. Visualize timings: Node A reads ten, pauses; Node B reads ten, increments to eleven and writes; Node A later writes eleven too, resulting in only one increment applied. Next, propose a distributed lock solution: use a lock key scoped to the counter, attempt to acquire the lock with a safe algorithm such as SET if not exists with an expiry, or use a consensus-backed lock service for stronger guarantees. When a node acquires the lock it reads the counter, performs the increment, writes the new value, and releases the lock. Important operational details: set a lock timeout to avoid indefinite holds, verify ownership before deletion to avoid deleting someone else's lock, and use fencing tokens when writes are made to resources that do not check lock ownership. Also include retry jitter for nodes that fail to acquire the lock to avoid thundering herd. Finally reflect: ask whether the outbox or CRDT approaches could eliminate the lock in your application. The exercise teaches both diagnosis and a defensible solution you can explain in interviews.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Simulate & Lock
Step 1: Illustrate the race
Two nodes both read the counter at 10 and intend to increment. Without coordination both may write 11, losing one increment.
Step 2: Lock-based solution
  • Attempt to acquire a lock key for the counter using a safe algorithm with expiry.
  • If lock acquired, read counter, increment, write, then release the lock after verifying ownership.
  • If lock not acquired, wait with randomized backoff and retry to avoid contention spikes.
Operational checklist
Use lock timeouts, ownership checks, fencing tokens, and jittered retries to be robust under failures.
Reflection
Consider CRDTs or owner-routing of writes if the lock causes a throughput bottleneck or single-point contention.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, concurrency is interleaving of tasks and parallelism is true simultaneous work; both are relevant in distributed systems and require different design thinking. Second, race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks are common hazards when multiple actors modify shared state; identify shared mutable state early. Third, local primitives like mutexes and atomic operations are powerful on one host but need careful translation to distributed coordination. Fourth, distributed locks, when necessary, must include timeouts, ownership verification, and fencing tokens to remain safe. Fifth, eventual consistency and CRDTs provide models that favor availability and automatic reconciliation, useful when temporary divergence is acceptable. Sixth, practical patterns such as the transactional outbox help achieve atomic intent between state updates and external messaging. Keep these concepts linked: detect shared state, pick the weakest consistency that meets correctness needs, and design for partial failures and monitoring. These rules form a practical checklist for interviews and real system designs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of concurrency and parallelism as they appear in distributed systems. You will learn the precise difference between handling many tasks at once by interleaving steps versus performing work truly simultaneously, and why both matter when services span multiple machines. We'll explore common hazards—race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks—by walking through short, concrete examples that show how shared state goes wrong. Then we'll move to synchronization strategies: how local locks, distributed locks, and higher-level models like eventual consistency and conflict-free replicated data types let systems stay available while avoiding incorrect results. Finally you'll see patterns engineers use in practice, such as the transactional outbox, and a checklist for spotting when shared mutable state should be redesigned or guarded. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to identify concurrency risks in a distributed design and propose appropriate synchronization or consistency techniques. Think of this chapter as a toolkit: definitions, examples, and proven patterns you can apply during design interviews and real system work.

These learning objectives guide our practical work. First, you'll be able to differentiate concurrency and parallelism in a system design context: describe how interleaving differs from true simultaneous execution and why that distinction changes your coordination choices. Second, you'll identify common concurrency hazards—race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks—by recognizing their symptomatic patterns and the typical causes when shared mutable state exists across threads or nodes. Third, you'll explain synchronization mechanisms: when to use locks, semaphores, or atomic operations on a single machine, and when distributed lock services or consensus are required. Fourth, you'll describe how distributed systems manage concurrency through distributed locks, eventual consistency, and CRDTs, and choose between them depending on availability and correctness requirements. Each objective pairs a skill with a short scenario so you can practice applying the concept to design decisions. By the end, you will not only name these techniques but also weigh trade-offs and recommend concrete solutions for interview-style problems.

This second objectives page focuses on practical application. You'll practice diagnosing interview-style scenarios: spotting shared mutable state, deciding whether a lock or a consistency model is needed, and proposing a safe, available approach. For example, given two services updating the same product stock, you should recognize a race condition risk and justify a distributed lock or a redesign to remove shared writes. You'll also practice trade-offs: when eventual consistency or CRDTs are acceptable, and when strong coherence is required, like in financial systems. Finally we'll train you to propose concrete engineering choices: a lock service with fencing tokens, or an outbox pattern for safe messaging. These skills let you present clear, defensible choices in an interview and avoid common mistakes in real systems. By the end you will be able to map a system requirement to a concurrency control plan that balances correctness and availability.

Start by anchoring the two terms with clear, practical definitions. Concurrency is the system's ability to manage multiple tasks such that progress appears to happen at the same time; this is often achieved by interleaving work on a single processor or coordinating many tasks so the system is responsive. Parallelism is the true simultaneous execution of tasks using multiple processing units or machines. In practice, a web service uses concurrency to handle many client requests at once by switching between request handlers, while a batch job uses parallelism to split a large dataset across nodes for simultaneous processing. This distinction affects correctness and coordination because concurrency introduces interleaving that creates ordering uncertainty, while parallelism adds capacity and true simultaneous mutation possibility across independent processors. A common misconception is to believe that adding more threads or nodes automatically eliminates race conditions; it doesn't. If multiple workers modify the same shared value, interleaving or simultaneous execution can both produce incorrect final state unless guarded. As a quick example, consider a counter service: concurrency lets many requests be handled quickly but requires synchronization to avoid lost increments; parallelism scales throughput but also multiplies the need for coordination. The takeaway is simple: name the mode your design needs, then pick the coordination model that provides the required correctness guarantees.

A race condition happens when the final outcome depends on the unpredictable order or timing of operations by concurrent actors. The essential characteristic is that two or more actors read and write the same mutable state without proper coordination. A typical illustration: two nodes attempt to increment a shared counter. Both read the same initial value, each computes the updated value, and each writes back. If the writes are not serialized, one increment can overwrite the other, leaving the counter lower than expected. This is not a timing bug only; it is a correctness bug rooted in shared mutable state. Concrete example: imagine a database counter at value ten. Node A reads ten and computes eleven, then pauses. Node B also reads ten and computes eleven, then writes eleven. When A resumes it writes eleven too. The system ends up at eleven instead of twelve. Common misconceptions include assuming database writes are atomic across reads and writes or believing that network latency only causes performance issues rather than correctness ones. To prevent races in single-process programs we use locks, atomic operations, or transactions. In distributed systems, an additional layer is needed: distributed locks or models that avoid shared mutable writes entirely, such as CRDTs or designing operations to be idempotent. The key takeaway: locate shared mutable state and force a single authoritative update path or use a mergeable model to avoid lost updates.

Two additional hazards often appear when multiple actors coordinate: deadlocks and livelocks. A deadlock occurs when two or more processes each hold resources the others need and wait indefinitely; no one can make progress. A classic two-resource deadlock: process one holds resource A and waits for B while process two holds B and waits for A. That cycle of waiting is the defining pattern. Livelock looks similar but is distinguished by continuous state changes that nevertheless yield no forward progress; processes keep reacting to each other without making the intended updates. An example is two networked services that repeatedly back off and retry in reaction to each other's retries, never completing the operation. To avoid deadlocks, focus on resource ordering: impose a global order for acquiring locks so cycles cannot form, or use try-lock with rollback and retry logic. To mitigate livelock, introduce randomized backoff or change retry strategies so actors do not tightly synchronize their retries. In distributed systems, partial failures and network delays can turn benign lock sequences into deadlocks if timeouts are neglected. A common misconception is treating timeouts as mere performance knobs; they are essential safety mechanisms. The core takeaway: reason about progress and ordering, and design global acquisition rules or timeout-based recovery to preserve forward progress.

Synchronization primitives are the building blocks that prevent concurrent hazards on a single machine. Mutual exclusion locks or mutexes let only one thread enter a critical section at a time. Semaphores generalize this by allowing a fixed number of concurrent holders. Atomic operations, such as compare-and-swap, give lock-free guarantees for certain updates. While these primitives solve many problems on one host, they do not automatically work across machines: memory is local, and network partitions, latency, and partial failures break assumptions. For distributed coordination you need a shared, reliable service or a consensus mechanism that provides a consistent view of lock ownership. Another important limitation is performance: fine-grained locking can hurt throughput and increase contention; coarse-grained locking simplifies correctness but reduces parallelism. Deadlocks and priority inversion remain concerns even with correct locking. A recommended pattern is to minimize shared mutable state: prefer immutable messages, owner-based routing of writes, or partitioning so locks are local to a shard. When distributed locking is unavoidable, design for failure: use timeouts, fencing tokens to prevent stale lock holders from acting, and ensure the lock service itself is highly available and consistent. This mindset helps you judge when to use primitives and when to adopt alternative models.

Distributed locks extend the mutual exclusion concept across machines by using a centralized or consensus-backed service to grant ownership. Typical implementations use ZooKeeper, etcd, or Redis with a carefully designed algorithm. The basic workflow: a client requests a lock from the lock service, which grants ownership if the lock is free. The client performs the critical update while holding the lock, then releases it. Several pitfalls must be considered. First, the lock service must itself be highly available; if it fails, the system may block. Second, network partitions and client crashes can leave stale locks. To mitigate stale-holders performing banned operations after a timeout, fencing tokens are used: when a client acquires the lock it receives a monotonically increasing token from the lock service and includes it with its write. Lock-aware resources reject writes that carry older tokens. A common mistake is naive lock release: clients should only release locks they own, and implementations must verify ownership before deleting lock keys. If you use Redis, patterns like SETNX with expirations are simple but require care: ensure clock skew and expiry races are handled, or prefer a consensus-backed store for strict correctness. The practical takeaway is to prefer distributed locks when you must serialize access across nodes, and to pair locks with timeouts, fencing, and ownership checks to remain robust in the face of failures.

Consistency models govern the guarantees a system provides about reads after writes. Strong consistency guarantees that once a write completes, all subsequent reads will see that write. Eventual consistency relaxes this by guaranteeing that if no new updates are made, replicas will converge to the same value eventually. The trade-off is the familiar CAP tension: prioritizing availability and partition tolerance often requires relaxing immediate consistency. Which model you choose depends on your application's correctness needs. For social features such as like counts or view counters, eventual consistency is acceptable because temporary divergence is harmless and availability is important. Conversely, financial account balances demand strong consistency because even a small window of divergence can lead to incorrect balances or double-spends. A misconception is to treat eventual consistency as sloppy design; it is instead a deliberate choice that trades immediate coherence for availability and performance, often combined with conflict-resolution strategies. When using eventual consistency, pair it with monitoring and clear user expectations: show eventual values in UIs or provide conflict resolution semantics. The takeaway: pick the weakest consistency that still meets correctness requirements to maximize availability and performance.

CRDTs are specially designed data types that can be replicated across multiple nodes and concurrently updated while guaranteeing that replicas converge without coordination. The key idea is to design merge rules that are associative, commutative, and idempotent so that the order of operations doesn't matter for the final state. Examples include grow-only counters, last-writer-wins registers, and sets with well-defined merge behavior. In a collaborative editor, CRDTs allow multiple users to edit simultaneously and have edits merged automatically without a global lock. The major advantage of CRDTs is availability: nodes can accept writes locally even during partitions and later reconcile deterministically. The trade-offs are complexity and sometimes imprecise semantics—some CRDTs, like last-writer-wins, discard information based on timestamps, which may be undesirable for some domains. Another misconception is thinking CRDTs replace all coordination; they are ideal when merge semantics fit application correctness. When strict serializability is required, CRDTs are not a substitute. The practical rule: when you can express your update intent as a mergeable operation and can tolerate the CRDT's semantics, they greatly simplify distributed concurrency by removing the need for synchronous locks.

The transactional outbox pattern solves a common distributed problem: ensuring a state update and an external message publication occur atomically. In many services you must update local state and then publish an event to a message broker; doing those operations separately can lead to inconsistencies if one succeeds and the other fails. The outbox pattern records the outgoing message in a local outbox table inside the same database transaction as the state change. After the transaction commits, a separate reliable process reads pending outbox entries and publishes them to the message broker, deleting entries only after successful publication. This decouples the atomicity of the state change from the eventual act of publishing, while guaranteeing that messages are not lost or duplicated beyond what the publisher handles. Important operational notes: the outbox reader must handle retries and idempotency, and visibility to the message system must be monitored. A common misconception is that the outbox removes the need for idempotent consumers; it does not — consumers still need to tolerate duplicates if the publisher retries. The practical outcome is a simpler failure model: updates are durable and messages are eventually published, letting services coordinate without distributed transactions across services.

When presented with a system design or interview scenario, follow a short checklist to identify concurrency concerns and choose an appropriate mitigation. First, detect shared mutable state: ask which data items have multiple writers and where single writers could be introduced. Second, assess correctness requirements: does the application tolerate eventual convergence or require immediate consistency? Third, consider scale and latency: will locking degrade throughput or produce hotspots? Fourth, evaluate failure modes: what happens if a lock holder crashes or a network partition occurs? Based on these answers, recommend either local synchronization (if the problem is single-node), a distributed lock with fencing (if serialization across nodes is essential), or a consistency-based redesign such as CRDTs, owner-based writes, or the transactional outbox. A concrete example: two microservices updating a product's stock concurrently. Detect that both write the same field. If immediate consistency is required, propose a distributed lock keyed by product id and explain fencing and timeout handling. If availability is prioritized and small discrepancies are acceptable, suggest an eventual model or partitioned ownership per product shard. Finally, verify your choice by outlining recovery steps for crashes and how to monitor integrity. The takeaway is to follow a repeatable checklist to produce a defensible recommendation.

Engineers often make a small set of recurring mistakes when reasoning about distributed concurrency. One is assuming networked operations are atomic; a write to a remote database may succeed on one replica and fail on another, producing partial effects. Another is neglecting partial failure: a client may acquire a lock then crash, leaving the resource held unless leases and timeouts are used. A third mistake is underestimating message ordering and latency—assuming a later update cannot overtake an earlier one across replicas. To avoid these, explicitly model failure modes in your design: what happens if a leader crashes, a lock service becomes unavailable, or messages reorder? Use timeouts and fencing for locks, ensure idempotent operations and at-least-once or exactly-once publishing where appropriate, and monitor for anomalies in replica divergence. Common quick checks in reviews include asking how ownership is transferred, how stale writers are protected against, and whether your design permits lost updates under high latency. A useful safety principle is to minimize shared mutable state or confine it to a single owner when possible. When unavoidable, build defensive patterns: timeouts, fencing tokens, transactional outbox, and observability to detect when models diverge. The core message: designing for failure is the point of distributed concurrency planning.

This activity guides you through a conceptual simulation and a lock-based solution for a distributed counter. First, illustrate the race: two nodes read the same counter value, compute increments, and write without coordination, producing a lost update. Visualize timings: Node A reads ten, pauses; Node B reads ten, increments to eleven and writes; Node A later writes eleven too, resulting in only one increment applied. Next, propose a distributed lock solution: use a lock key scoped to the counter, attempt to acquire the lock with a safe algorithm such as SET if not exists with an expiry, or use a consensus-backed lock service for stronger guarantees. When a node acquires the lock it reads the counter, performs the increment, writes the new value, and releases the lock. Important operational details: set a lock timeout to avoid indefinite holds, verify ownership before deletion to avoid deleting someone else's lock, and use fencing tokens when writes are made to resources that do not check lock ownership. Also include retry jitter for nodes that fail to acquire the lock to avoid thundering herd. Finally reflect: ask whether the outbox or CRDT approaches could eliminate the lock in your application. The exercise teaches both diagnosis and a defensible solution you can explain in interviews.

Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, concurrency is interleaving of tasks and parallelism is true simultaneous work; both are relevant in distributed systems and require different design thinking. Second, race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks are common hazards when multiple actors modify shared state; identify shared mutable state early. Third, local primitives like mutexes and atomic operations are powerful on one host but need careful translation to distributed coordination. Fourth, distributed locks, when necessary, must include timeouts, ownership verification, and fencing tokens to remain safe. Fifth, eventual consistency and CRDTs provide models that favor availability and automatic reconciliation, useful when temporary divergence is acceptable. Sixth, practical patterns such as the transactional outbox help achieve atomic intent between state updates and external messaging. Keep these concepts linked: detect shared state, pick the weakest consistency that meets correctness needs, and design for partial failures and monitoring. These rules form a practical checklist for interviews and real system designs.

These three compact reminders are practical anchors for interviews or quick design checks. First, always identify shared mutable state: if multiple writers exist, plan coordination or redesign. Second, choose the weakest consistency model that meets correctness: use eventual consistency or CRDTs where divergence is acceptable, and locks or consensus when strict correctness is required. Third, when using distributed locks, include timeouts, fencing tokens, and ownership verification to protect against stale clients and partial failures. Use these as a short checklist when reviewing designs: detect, choose model, and harden for failures. One last reflective question: given a problem in an interview, which of these three cards drives your primary decision, and why? That reflection helps you present clear trade-offs under time pressure.
